rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds while revealing retention and critical separation regions. A midrange temperature leaves room to optimize selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin can be retained. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

A 12-minute gradient should recover some resolution in the crowded middle region while keeping the last peak near the apparent zero-time-penalty boundary. This brackets the tradeoff before changing temperature to improve selectivity.
Raise temperature at the same gradient to test whether selectivity improves the single critical pair. Faster elution may also create room for a shallower gradient without a time penalty.

The middle-peak pattern suggests an elution-order reversal between 40 and 50 C, so another 5 C increase may open the critical pair. Test 55 C while monitoring the narrowing earlier pair, with the last peak expected to remain within the zero-time-penalty region.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient for an alternative with greater separation margin. This will reveal whether the two critical pairs improve together while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty region.

Keep the maximum-scoring method as the benchmark and test a higher starting organic fraction as an independent selectivity adjustment. This may shorten retention while revealing whether both critical pairs can retain baseline resolution.

Combine the higher starting organic fraction with a longer gradient to recover the earlier critical separation. The observed trends suggest both critical pairs could exceed 1.5 while the last peak remains within the zero-time-penalty region.

Test whether another increase in starting organic fraction, offset by a longer gradient, further improves the minimum resolution. Injection 8 supports this direction, and the last peak is expected to remain below approximately 9 minutes without a time penalty.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 8 to improve the earlier critical pair while testing whether the later pair retains resolution above 1.5. The predicted last-peak time remains below 9 minutes, making this a promising additional maximum-score method.

This gradient slope lies between injections 7 and 8, targeting a better balance between the two critical separations. It may preserve the maximum CRF while eluting the last peak slightly earlier than injection 8.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 9 to bring its earlier critical pair above 1.5 while retaining the later pair’s larger margin. This tests another potential maximum-score method, although the last peak may approach the time-penalty boundary.

Use a slightly steeper slope than injection 11 to balance its two critical pairs more closely and shorten retention. Both separations are predicted to remain above 1.5, potentially preserving the maximum CRF with a modestly shorter run.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a cooler, faster alternative rather than further tuning equivalent 55 C methods. Lower temperature may reverse the middle-cluster selectivity enough to resolve the short-gradient overlap, though other pairs must be checked.

Preserve injection 5’s gradient slope through the critical middle peaks, then hold at 50% organic to test a lower-solvent alternative. The key uncertainty is whether the last compound still elutes before the time penalty begins; the maximum-scoring benchmark remains available.

Preserve injection 11’s slope and critical-pair separations while ending the gradient at 60% organic. The last peak should elute before the gradient ends, making this a likely maximum-CRF alternative with a lower final organic fraction.

Retain injection 5’s successful gradient slope while reducing the endpoint to 65% organic. Since its last peak eluted before this gradient would finish at the outlet, this method is expected to preserve the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test the upper temperature limit to map selectivity beyond 55 C. The longer gradient provides some margin for the earlier critical pair while higher temperature may improve the later pair.

Test a substantially faster gradient and higher starting organic fraction at 60 C to explore separation beyond the earlier pair’s apparent order reversal. This is an exploratory shorter-run alternative; the established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmarks.

Increase starting organic fraction to test whether the reversed critical pair separates further, while lengthening the gradient to protect neighboring separations. This explores a potentially faster maximum-score alternative to the established 55 C methods.

Return to the proven 55 C region and test a shallower gradient with a lower endpoint. Trends predict both critical resolutions above 1.5 and the last peak near 8.8 minutes, potentially retaining CRF 1.000 at 55% final organic.

Use the same gradient slope as injection 5 with an intermediate endpoint, providing another expected maximum-CRF method. All peaks should elute before the endpoint affects the chromatogram; the campaign has already reached the score ceiling.

Test a slope between injections 8 and 10, both of which achieved the maximum CRF. This should retain baseline resolution for all pairs and keep the last peak below 9 minutes, adding another maximum-score option.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 13 with a 50% organic hold, targeting a shorter, lower-endpoint alternative. The earlier critical pair may fall just below 1.5, so this probes the edge of the maximum-score region while retaining the proven methods.

Use the final injection to test the same slope as injection 24 without its low-organic hold, checking whether continued gradient elution changes the borderline separation. The campaign’s maximum CRF of 1.000 is already secured by injection 5 and multiple alternatives.
